newsitem.title: CANADA: Robert Bourassa, former Quebec premier, dead at 63.
newsitem.headline: Robert Bourassa, former Quebec premier, dead at 63.

text.p: Former Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa died early on Wednesday in Notre-Dame hospital in Montreal after a six-year battle with cancer, hospital officials said. He was 63.
"It is with regret that I announce that Robert Bourassa died at 5:45 a.m. EDT (0945 GMT)," Notre-Dame spokeswoman Anne-Marie Tardif said.

Bourassa had been admitted to Notre-Dame on Aug. 17 to undergo treatment for melanoma, or skin cancer, that had spread to other parts of his body. Hospital officials said Bourassa had suffered a relapse.
Bourassa's doctor, Joseph Ayoub, told reporters that Bourassa lapsed into unconsciousness Tuesday afternoon.
"He said he was ready for the big fight. He was not afraid of death," Ayoub said.

Flags flew at half-staff in Quebec City, the capital of this French-speaking province of 7.3 million people, as the provincial legislature mourned Bourassa and tributes from Bourassa's friends, political allies and foes poured in.
Lucien Bouchard, the separatist Parti Quebecois premier of Quebec, told reporters that Quebec had offered a state funeral for Bourassa.
Bouchard paid tribute to Bourassa's ability to appeal to a cross-section of Quebec voters, perhaps reflecting Quebec's "ambiguity" on the issue of Canadian unity.
In Ottawa, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said Bourassa was "great servant of the state."
"Canada has lost one of its major political figures. Mr. Bourassa left his mark on the modern history of Quebec and the whole country," Chretien said.

"Few public figures of his generation have dedicated so much intelligence, perseverance and courage to the defence of his compatriots' interests and the illustration of his country's greatness," said former Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney.

During his two terms as premier, from 1970 to 1976 and from 1985 to 1994, Bourassa was an ardent defender of Canadian unity and strove to keep Quebec in Canada. But he was also a pragmatic Quebec nationalist who took controversial measures to protect and promote the French language, spoken by the vast majority of Quebec residents.

Bourassa also promoted the province's economic growth and the emergence of a French-speaking business class. He spurred the development of Quebec's hydroelectric resources in remote northern parts of the province and was instrumental in promoting North American free trade.

The lanky, bespectacled politician was premier during some of the most tumultuous periods of Quebec's recent political history. Shortly after taking office for the first time, in 1970, he was confronted with the "October Crisis," when the left-wing, nationalist Front de Liberation du Quebec kidnapped the British trade commissioner and a Quebec Cabinet minister.
The trade commissioner, James Cross, was released, but the body of the Cabinet minister, Pierre Laporte, was found in the trunk of a car near Montreal.

Bourassa was re-elected in 1973, but his Liberal Party government was driven from office in 1976 by the separatist Parti Quebecois under charismatic one-time journalist and former Quebec Liberal Cabinet minister Rene Levesque.
But he staged a remarkable comeback in 1983, regaining the leadership of the Quebec Liberals. He won the premiership two years later. Bourassa resigned in January 1994 because of his cancer.
